scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

prediction.raw: **N** (Not the Asshole) **Here’s why, with clear reasoning:** ### 1. **You did nothing wrong.** - You were working in a designated space (the dining room) as part of your job. This is *your* workspace, not a "private family area" you were exploiting. - Your parents chose to escalate their argument **in a shared hallway** during work hours, fully visible to your camera (which was *on you*, not them). **They walked into your workspace uninvited**—this is on *them*, not you. - You handled it professionally: - You paused the meeting calmly ("Hold on, can you still hear me?"). - You asked them to quiet down ("Hey, could y’all keep it down? Blaming *you* for their own lack of awareness is gaslighting. ### 3. **Their reaction is abusive and unreasonable.** - Kicking you out of your *own home* (where you’re living temporarily due to housing insecurity) because *they* caused a scene is cruel and irresponsible. - They’re treating you as the "problem" for exposing *their* dysfunction. This is classic toxic behavior: - **They created the chaos.** - **They refused to take accountability.** - **They punished *you* for their own actions.** - Demanding an apology for something you didn’t do is emotional manipulation. You have zero obligation to apologize for protecting your work environment. ### 4. **The bigger picture matters:** - You’re a young adult living with parents due to *external circumstances* (landlord selling the building, housing crisis). This is a temporary situation, and you’re about to move out in a month. - Your parents’ behavior—arguing loudly in a shared space during work hours, then blaming you—is **unhealthy and exploitative**. They’re prioritizing their ego over your well-being. - If they truly cared about "privacy," they wouldn’t have screamed in the hallway during your work meeting. The fact that they’re now weaponizing this to kick you out shows their priorities are warped. ### What you should do: - **Do NOT apologize.** You did nothing wrong. Apologizing would validate their false narrative and reward their abusive behavior. - **Set boundaries:** When you return home (if you choose to), say: > *"I understand you’re upset, but I was working in my designated space. If you need privacy, please use your own rooms or wait until I’m not working. I won’t tolerate being yelled at or kicked out for your arguments."* - **Document everything:** If they continue this behavior, save texts/emails showing their threats (e.g., "You’ll have to leave"). This protects you legally if they try to force you out before your lease starts. - **Prioritize your safety:** If they’re volatile, stay at the hotel until you move out. You don’t owe them your peace. ### Why this isn’t your fault: > **Dysfunctional families often turn victims into scapegoats.** Your parents’ anger isn’t about the meeting—it’s about being exposed. Their shame about their own behavior is being projected onto you. **You’re not responsible for their choices.** This isn’t "AITA." **They’re the assholes.** Stay firm, stay calm, and focus on moving out in a month. You’ve handled this with maturity—they haven’t. *(Note: If you feel unsafe, reach out to a trusted friend, counselor, or local support services. You deserve respect.)* 💛
